# The Lost Art of Being Lost

Somewhere in the pocket of nearly everyone alive today sits a device that has quietly abolished one of the oldest human experiences: not knowing where you are. The blue dot glides across the map; the voice says "turn left in two hundred meters"; and when we disobey, it sighs and begins *recalculating*—a word that has become the soundtrack of modern movement. We arrive, mostly, on time. And something, I think, has gone missing.

For most of human history, navigation was a form of reading. The Marshall Islanders of Micronesia crossed hundreds of miles of open Pacific in outrigger canoes, guided by stick charts—lattices of palm ribs and cowrie shells that encoded the patterns of ocean swells, the way waves refract and bend around islands too distant to see. Navigators learned to feel these rhythms through their bodies, lying in the hull to sense how the sea was leaning. They read the stars, the flight paths of birds at dusk, the color of clouds over lagoons, which turn faintly green where shallow water reflects upward. To be a navigator was to hold the ocean in your mind as a living text.

Meanwhile in Europe, maps were for a long time not really about geography at all. The Hereford Mappa Mundi, drawn around 1300 on a single sheet of calfskin, places Jerusalem at the center of the world and paradise at the top, at the eastern edge. It is less a tool for travel than a diagram of salvation history—the world arranged as an argument about God. You could not have navigated to the corner market with it. That wasn't the point.

The practical turn came with the portolan charts of the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries: dense webs of rhumb lines radiating from compass roses, coastlines of the Mediterranean rendered with an accuracy that still startles historians, because no one knows quite how they did it. Then, in 1569, Gerardus Mercator published his famous projection—a mathematical miracle for sailors, since a line of constant bearing becomes a straight line on the map—and a quiet catastrophe for everyone's sense of proportion. On Mercator's map, Greenland looms the size of Africa, though Africa is roughly fourteen times larger. Every map is a trade: you keep one truth and sacrifice another. There is no innocent map, only maps that are honest about their distortions and maps that aren't.

Borges pushed this to its limit in a one-paragraph story about an empire whose cartographers, drunk on rigor, built a map the exact size of the empire itself, point for point. Later generations, less devoted, abandoned it to the weather, and its tattered ruins still shelter beggars and animals in the western deserts. The joke cuts deep: a perfect map is useless precisely because it is perfect. Maps matter only insofar as they are smaller than the world—insofar as they leave things out. Forgetting is the cartographer's first tool.

Which brings me to the hippocampus, the seahorse-shaped curl of brain tissue where, among other things, we keep our maps. In a famous series of studies, neuroscientist Eleanor Maguire scanned the brains of London taxi drivers—men and women who spend years mastering "the Knowledge," the layout of some 25,000 streets—and found their posterior hippocampi enlarged, growing with years on the job. The brain, it seems, builds itself out of the streets it memorizes. And the reverse appears to hold as well: studies of habitual GPS users find weaker spatial memory and less hippocampal engagement, as if the skill, unexercised, quietly withers. When we outsource navigation to the blue dot, we are not merely saving time. We are declining to build a part of ourselves.

I don't want to romanticize lostness too much. Being lost at sea without water is not a spiritual exercise; being lost in a strange city at midnight with a dead phone is mostly just frightening. But there is a gentler species of being lost—the wrong turn in a town you're visiting, the unplanned hour—that functions as a kind of forced attention. When you don't know where you are, you actually look. You notice the bakery, the strange church, the cat on the windowsill, because you need the world in a way the guided traveler never does. Serendipity is not really luck; it is what attention feels like from the inside. The blue dot is excellent at getting you to your destination and terrible at letting the destination find you.

There is also something to be said for what getting lost teaches about scale and humility. To be lost is to be briefly returned to the actual size of the world—to feel that the territory exceeds your map of it, that the grid in your head is a sketch and not the thing itself. Medieval mapmakers were said to mark the edges of the known with the legend *hic sunt dracones*, here be dragons, and while the phrase is largely a myth—it appears on exactly one surviving globe—the sentiment is true to life: the unknown has always had teeth. GPS promises a world with no edges, no dragons, no blank spaces. But a world with no blank spaces is a world with nowhere for surprise to live.

So here is my modest proposal, offered in the spirit of someone who loves maps too much to want them abolished: occasionally, on purpose, turn the thing off. Pick a direction and walk. Let the city or the countryside be bigger than your plan for it. Keep the phone in your pocket as a rope back to the known world if you like—even the Polynesian navigators carried the memory of home as their deepest instrument. But give yourself an hour in which you do not know, precisely, where you are, and see what your attention does with the freedom.

The old maps were wrong in wonderful ways. The new ones are right in narrowing ones. Somewhere between the mappa mundi and the blue dot, there is a way of moving through the world that keeps both the precision and the wonder. I suspect it begins with the willingness, now and then, to be a little bit lost—and to notice, while you're at it, the greenish tint of a cloud that means land is near.
